text:
A Roth IRA (Roth individual retirement account) is a U.S. retirement savings account funded with after-tax dollars where investments grow tax-free and qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free.
Key Rules & Features
After-Tax Contributions: You do not get an upfront tax deduction when you contribute money, unlike a traditional IRA.
2026 Contribution Limits: You can contribute up to $7,500 in 2026 if you are under age 50, or $8,600 if you are 50 or older, provided you have qualifying earned income.
2026 Income Limits: Your ability to contribute phases out based on modified adjusted gross income (MAGI). For 2026, full contributions apply below $153,000 for single filers (phasing out completely at $168,000) and below $242,000 for married couples filing jointly (phasing out completely at $252,000).
Tax-Free Withdrawals: Original contributions can be withdrawn anytime tax- and penalty-free. Investment earnings can be withdrawn tax- and penalty-free once you reach age 59½ and have held the account for at least five tax years.
No Required Minimum Distributions (RMDs): Unlike traditional IRAs, original account owners do not have to take mandatory withdrawals during their lifetime.
Usage Examples & Synonyms
Usage Examples:
"A 24-year-old in a low tax bracket opens a Fidelity Roth IRA to lock in today's tax rate and let decades of investment growth compound tax-free."
"Because she has already contributed $8,000 and earned $22,000 in gains over more than five years, she can withdraw her earnings tax-free after age 59½."
"Even though his employer offers a 401(k), he contributes to a Roth IRA on his own through Charles Schwab while under the income limit."
Synonyms & Related Terms:
Roth individual retirement account
After-tax IRA (informal)
Related (not exact synonyms): Traditional IRA, Roth 401(k), SEP IRA.
